hist.biblio1.4.dit: A pipe, now! `cat` reads the whole book, and `|` sends its lines to `grep`, which keeps only the ones where Abyssor sleeps.
hist.biblio1.4.bravo: Your first pipe! The lines flowed from `cat` to `grep`. Watch them go by in the unfolded view.
hist.biblio1.4.adulte: `|` (pipe) connects one command's output to the next one's input: `cat file | grep word` is the same here as `grep word file`.
hist.port.debut: ⚓ Welcome to the Harbour! Here, every biome of the Terminaworld is a machine with its own address, and little messengers carry packets from one to another. We'll find our address, read the directory, send the postman and light our own lighthouse.
hist.port.fin: All the lighthouses are shining! You know where each machine lives, how messengers travel and how to recognise a real seal. You are Harbour Captain.
port.ouvert.log: 🌍 A world opens at the Crossroads: the Harbour
port.ouvert.dit: You can read, search and connect pipes: the Harbour opens its docks to you! Whenever you like: `cd ~/terrain_terminagotchi/port`.
hist.port1.titre: Who am I on the network?
hist.port0.1.dit: Look at what's on the docks: `ls`.
hist.port0.1.bravo: A sign, the harbour directory, the logbook, your dock and the teleporter. Let's visit it all!
hist.port0.1.adulte: `ls` lists the port folder the game prepared in your play area; the game writes nothing elsewhere.
hist.port0.2.bravo: The captain was waiting for you! Every biome is a machine, and every machine has an address.
hist.port0.2.adulte: The Harbour simulates a small network of 11 machines at 127.x.x.x addresses: these are loopback addresses, nothing leaves your computer.
hist.port1.0.dit: Every machine has a name. What is yours called? `hostname`.
hist.port1.0.bravo: That's your computer's name on the network. Other machines can call it that.
hist.port1.0.adulte: `hostname` prints the system's host name (/etc/hostname on Linux). A name is not an address: you need a directory to go from one to the other.
hist.port1.1.dit: And your address? The network cards are in `ip a`. Look for lo and 127.0.0.1.
hist.port1.1.bravo: lo is the loop: a card that only leads back to yourself. 127.0.0.1 is your base camp: localhost.
hist.port1.1.adulte: `ip a` (ip address) lists the interfaces with their IPv4 (inet) and IPv6 (inet6) addresses. lo is the loopback interface: 127.0.0.1/8, the whole 127.0.0.0 to 127.255.255.255 block.
hist.port1.2.dit: Shout "Ahoy!" towards your own camp: `ping -c 3 localhost`.
hist.port1.2.bravo: 3 echoes sent, 3 came back: 0% loss. The time in ms is the round trip.
hist.port1.2.adulte: ping sends ICMP Echo requests and measures the reply time; -c 3 stops after 3. Towards localhost, packets never leave the machine.
hist.port2.0.dit: Your computer has its own tiny directory: `cat /etc/hosts`.
hist.port2.0.bravo: You see localhost next to 127.0.0.1: the directory says which address goes with that name.
hist.port2.0.adulte: /etc/hosts maps names to addresses; it is checked before DNS (order set in /etc/nsswitch.conf). We only read it: it belongs to the guardian (root).
hist.port2.1.dit: Ask your computer for the address of the name localhost: `getent hosts localhost`.
hist.port2.1.bravo: It looked in the directory and answered with the address. Your browser does the same before every visit.
hist.port2.1.adulte: `getent hosts` queries the system's name databases (hosts file, then DNS) the way programs do. DNS does the same at Internet scale.
hist.port2.2.dit: The harbour directory knows every machine in the Terminaworld. Look for the Fire biome: `grep feu annuaire.txt`.
hist.port2.2.bravo: feu.terminaworld lives at 127.42.0.2. Address on the left, name on the right, just like /etc/hosts.
hist.port2.2.adulte: annuaire.txt uses the /etc/hosts format. The 127.42.0.x addresses are in the loopback range: on Linux, `ping -c 1 127.42.0.2` answers, and nothing leaves the machine.
hist.port3.0.dit: The harbour lighthouse is a real little web server. Send the postman to ask for the envelope only: `curl -I http://localhost:8042/`.
hist.port3.0.bravo: HTTP/1.1 200 OK: "all good". Below, the headers: who answers, what kind of letter, its size.
hist.port3.0.adulte: `curl -I` sends a HEAD request: only the status line and the response headers. The lighthouse only listens on 127.0.0.1 (loopback).
hist.port3.1.dit: Now the letter itself, but only the beginning: `curl -s http://localhost:8042/eau | head -n 3`.
hist.port3.1.bravo: The postman brought back the Water biome's page, and the pipe kept only 3 lines.
hist.port3.1.adulte: Without -I, curl does a GET and writes the response body to its output; -s hides the progress bar; head -n 3 keeps 3 lines.
hist.port3.2.dit: Put a letter in your bag: `curl -o colis.html http://localhost:8042/feu`.
hist.port3.2.bravo: colis.html arrived on the dock. You can open it with cat.
hist.port3.2.adulte: -o writes the response body to a file instead of the screen: the postman drops off the parcel.
hist.port3.3.dit: And if we ask for a page that doesn't exist? `curl -I http://localhost:8042/volcan_perdu`.
hist.port3.3.bravo: 404 Not Found: the lighthouse did answer, but that page doesn't exist. The postman still comes back!
hist.port3.3.adulte: HTTP codes: 2xx success, 3xx redirection, 4xx client error (404: resource not found), 5xx server error.
hist.port4.0.dit: The ssh teleporter links two machines through a secret tunnel. What version is it? `ssh -V`.
hist.port4.0.bravo: OpenSSH is here. We won't teleport anywhere: we'll make the key.
hist.port4.0.adulte: ssh opens an encrypted session on another machine. `ssh -V` opens nothing: it only prints the version.
hist.port4.1.dit: Make your key pair, here in the harbour: `ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -N "" -C explorateur -f cle_du_port`.
hist.port4.1.bravo: Two files: cle_du_port, the secret key you must NEVER give away, and cle_du_port.pub, the padlock you can show.
hist.port4.1.adulte: ssh-keygen creates an Ed25519 pair: the private key (mode 600) and the public key (.pub). -N "": no passphrase, only for playing here; -C: a comment with no personal data.
hist.port4.2.dit: Look at the padlock, the public key: `cat cle_du_port.pub`.
hist.port4.2.bravo: ssh-ed25519, a long string of letters, then explorateur. That's what you put on a machine so it recognises you.
hist.port4.2.adulte: The public key is copied into ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on the target machine; the private key proves your identity without ever travelling.
hist.port5.0.dit: Write your dock's page: `echo "Bienvenue sur mon quai" > quai/index.html`.
hist.port5.0.bravo: Your page is ready. Now someone has to serve it.
hist.port5.0.adulte: index.html is the page a web server returns when a folder is requested.
hist.port5.1.dit: Light your lantern at dock 8000, just for you: `python3 -m http.server 8000 --bind 127.0.0.1 --directory quai &`.
hist.port5.1.bravo: Your lantern shines at dock 8000! Thanks to --bind 127.0.0.1, nobody else on the Wi-Fi can see it.
hist.port5.1.adulte: http.server serves the files of a folder. Without --bind it listens on every interface (0.0.0.0): any machine on the local network could read the folder. & runs it in the background.
hist.port5.2.bravo: "Bienvenue sur mon quai": your server answered. Your browser would do exactly the same.
hist.port5.2.adulte: curl plays the client and http.server the server: both are on your machine, linked by the loopback.
hist.port5.3.bravo: Lantern out. A server you no longer use should be stopped: one less open door.
hist.port5.3.adulte: %1 refers to job number 1 of this shell (the one started with &); kill sends it the SIGTERM signal.
hist.port6.0.dit: Watch the postman work in detail: `curl -v http://localhost:8042/`.
hist.port6.0.bravo: The "*" lines talk about the address and transport, the ">" lines are your letter, the "<" lines the reply. Several envelopes!
hist.port6.0.adulte: -v (verbose) shows the TCP connection (address and port), the HTTP request sent (>) and the headers received (<).
hist.port6.1.dit: Open the envelopes one by one: `port couches`.
hist.port6.1.bravo: The letter (application) inside the envelope (transport), inside the parcel (network), inside the truck (link).
hist.port6.1.adulte: The Internet model has 4 layers (RFC 1122); the OSI model has 7. Each layer adds its header around the data of the layer above.
hist.port6.2.dit: Write the 4 layers in order, from the letter to the truck: `echo "application transport reseau liaison" > couches.txt`.
hist.port6.2.bravo: In the right order! On arrival, you unpack the other way round: the truck first, the letter last.
hist.port6.2.adulte: Encapsulation when sending (application → link), decapsulation when receiving (link → application).
hist.port7.0.dit: Who is listening inside your computer? The open doors: `ss -tln`.
hist.port7.0.bravo: Each LISTEN line is an open door waiting for visitors: an address, a colon, a door number.
hist.port7.0.adulte: `ss -tln` lists TCP sockets (-t) that are listening (-l) without translating numbers (-n). 127.0.0.1:8042 only accepts local connections; 0.0.0.0 accepts the whole network.
hist.port7.1.dit: Find the lighthouse's door with a pipe: `ss -tln | grep 8042`.
hist.port7.1.bravo: 127.0.0.1:8042: dock 127.0.0.1, door 8042. An IP address plus a port is the full address of a service.
hist.port7.1.adulte: The IP address names the machine, the port (0 to 65535) the program listening. Ports below 1024 are reserved for system services.
hist.port7.2.dit: A machine can have several addresses. Note down all the Terminaworld's: `port carte`.
hist.port7.2.bravo: 11 machines, 11 addresses, and the lighthouses linking them. Your map is written in the logbook.
hist.port7.2.adulte: All these addresses are in 127.0.0.0/8: on Linux, your machine answers on each of them. A real machine can also have several cards and several addresses (IPv4 and IPv6).
hist.port8.0.bravo: TCP opens a connection, numbers the packets and waits for an acknowledgement for each one.
hist.port8.0.adulte: `ss -t` lists established TCP connections. TCP guarantees order and delivery (lost segments are resent): it carries the Web, ssh and e-mail.
hist.port8.1.bravo: UDP sends without a connection and without acknowledgements: fast, but nothing is guaranteed.
hist.port8.1.adulte: `ss -u` lists UDP sockets. UDP is used when speed matters more than a loss: DNS, online games, live voice and video.
hist.port8.2.dit: Start the race between the TCP messenger and the UDP messenger: `port course`.
hist.port8.2.bravo: TCP delivered everything in order by resending packets 2 and 5. UDP was faster, but lost 2 packets and mixed up 2.
hist.port8.2.adulte: Same network, same losses: TCP fixes them (retransmission, reordering), UDP leaves them to the application.
hist.port9.0.dit: Your computer has a map of routes: `ip route`.
hist.port9.0.bravo: The default via… line shows the gateway: the door through which every far-travelling messenger leaves.
hist.port9.0.adulte: `ip route` shows the routing table: for each destination, the interface and gateway to use. The default route covers everything else.
hist.port9.1.dit: Follow a messenger lighthouse by lighthouse to your own camp: `tracepath -n 127.0.0.1`.
hist.port9.1.bravo: Just one hop: your camp is right here! Towards a far-away site you'd see a dozen lighthouses.
hist.port9.1.adulte: tracepath sends packets with an increasing TTL; each router that brings the TTL down to 0 replies, which reveals the path. Towards a public site, only with an adult.
hist.port9.2.dit: Send a messenger from the camp to the Fire biome: `port messager feu`.
hist.port9.2.bravo: Camp → Root → Rock → Fire: 3 hops. At each lighthouse its time to live (TTL) drops by 1.
hist.port9.2.adulte: Each router picks the next hop from its routing table and decrements the TTL; at 0 the packet is dropped (no endless loop).
hist.port9.3.dit: Oh no, a storm! Turn off the Rock lighthouse: `port eteins roche`.
hist.port9.3.bravo: The Rock is in the dark. The usual path to Fire is cut: a detour is needed.
hist.port9.3.adulte: A router failure makes a route invalid; routing protocols (OSPF, BGP…) compute another path if one exists.
hist.port9.4.dit: Guide a messenger to Fire yourself without going through the Rock. Look at the map, then give the lighthouses in order: `port guide racine … feu`.
hist.port9.4.bravo: Arrived without loss! You found the detour lighthouse by lighthouse. A packet's path can change every time.
hist.port9.4.adulte: This is source routing: the sender sets the path. On the Internet, routers choose, hop by hop.
hist.port10.0.dit: Who is the caretaker of your home? Find the default route: `ip route | grep default`.
hist.port10.0.bravo: That address is your home router (or the school's): the building caretaker.
hist.port10.0.adulte: The default gateway is usually the home router, which is also the DHCP server and NAT for the local network.
hist.port10.1.dit: The neighbours your machine knows: `ip neigh`.
hist.port10.1.bravo: Each line links an IP address on the local network to a hardware (MAC) address. The caretaker is often there.
hist.port10.1.adulte: `ip neigh` shows the ARP/NDP table: the IP ↔ MAC address mapping of direct neighbours. A MAC address never leaves the local network.
hist.port10.2.dit: Watch the caretaker welcome new devices: `port gardien`.
hist.port10.2.bravo: The caretaker gives each one a flat number (DHCP) and posts all the mail with the building's address (NAT).
hist.port10.2.adulte: DHCP hands out private addresses (192.168.x.x, RFC 1918); NAT translates them into a single public address. 203.0.113.7 is an address reserved for documentation.
hist.port11.0.dit: The lighthouse also has a sealed door, over https. Knock: `curl https://localhost:8443`.
hist.port11.0.bravo: curl refuses: "self-signed certificate". The seal was signed by the lighthouse itself: nobody vouches for it.
hist.port11.0.adulte: With HTTPS the server presents a certificate; curl checks it is signed by a trusted authority and carries the right name. A self-signed certificate fails (error 60).
hist.port11.1.dit: The harbour notary gave you the lighthouse's seal. Tell curl to trust it: `curl --cacert sceau_du_phare.pem https://localhost:8443`.
hist.port11.1.bravo: This time the door opens: the seal matches the one you know. The letter travelled encrypted.
hist.port11.1.adulte: --cacert replaces the known authorities with this certificate. Only trust a certificate you received through a safe channel.
hist.port11.2.dit: The notary shows you 4 seals. Read them carefully: `port sceau`.
hist.port11.2.bravo: Look at who signed, for which name, and the date.
hist.port11.2.adulte: A valid certificate: signed by a recognised authority, for the exact site name, within its validity period.
hist.port11.3.dit: Which one is the real seal? Give its number: `port sceau ?`.
hist.port11.3.bravo: Well spotted! The padlock proves WHO you're talking to, not that what it says is true.
hist.port11.3.adulte: TLS guarantees the server's authenticity and the confidentiality of the trip; it says nothing about the site's honesty.
port.f.localhost.enfant: localhost is your base camp: an address that always leads back home.
port.f.localhost.grands: localhost (127.0.0.1, and ::1 in IPv6) means the machine itself; the whole 127.0.0.0/8 block stays inside the machine.
port.f.localhost.limite: The base camp is not a place on the network: a message sent to localhost goes through no cable.
port.f.localhost.idee: "127.0.0.1 is my computer's address on the Internet": no, every machine has its own loopback, which never leaves it.
port.f.hosts.enfant: The harbour directory: you give a name, it gives you the dock number.
port.f.hosts.grands: Name resolution turns a name into an IP address: the /etc/hosts file first, then DNS.
port.f.hosts.limite: A real phone book doesn't change every hour; DNS answers do: they have a time to live (TTL).
port.f.hosts.idee: "The name is enough to connect": no, the computer always needs the IP address.
port.f.http.enfant: curl is the postman: it carries your request and brings back the letter with its envelope.
port.f.http.grands: HTTP: a request (method, path, headers) and a response (status code, headers, body).
port.f.http.limite: The letter isn't paper: it's bytes, and the envelope (the headers) is text too.
port.f.http.idee: "404 means the site is down": no, the server answered; it's the page that doesn't exist.
port.f.ssh_cles.enfant: A secret key you always keep, and a padlock you can show everyone.
port.f.ssh_cles.grands: Public-key cryptography: what the public key can verify, only the private key can produce.
port.f.ssh_cles.limite: The padlock can be copied as much as you like, safely; the secret key never: whoever has it can pretend to be you.
port.f.ssh_cles.idee: "The public key must stay secret": no, it's the private key you protect.
port.f.serveur.enfant: A lantern on your dock: it answers whoever comes knocking.
port.f.serveur.grands: A server is a program that listens on an address and port and answers requests; bound to 127.0.0.1 it is invisible to the network.
port.f.serveur.limite: A server isn't necessarily a big machine: it's a role, and your computer can play it.
port.f.serveur.idee: "Only I can see my server": only if it listens on 127.0.0.1; on 0.0.0.0 the whole local network sees it.
port.f.couches.enfant: A letter in an envelope, in a parcel, in a truck.
port.f.couches.grands: The layered model: application, transport, network, link (the Internet's 4 layers; 7 in the OSI model).
port.f.couches.limite: Layers aren't objects: they're headers added around the data.
port.f.couches.idee: "The Internet and the Web are the same": no, the Web (HTTP) is only one application travelling over the Internet.
port.f.ports.enfant: The dock is the IP address; the warehouse door is the port number.
port.f.ports.grands: A socket = an IP address + a port (0 to 65535); a service listens on a port, and ss shows it.
port.f.ports.limite: A machine can have several addresses (several docks), and thousands of doors.
port.f.ports.idee: "An open port is a security hole": no, it's a listening service; the danger comes from a useless or badly protected service.
port.f.tcp_udp.enfant: TCP is the registered letter with proof of delivery; UDP is the postcard.
port.f.tcp_udp.grands: TCP: connection, acknowledgements, ordering, retransmission. UDP: independent datagrams, no guarantee.
port.f.tcp_udp.limite: "Lost" doesn't mean "stolen": a lost packet was dropped, for example by an overloaded router.
port.f.tcp_udp.idee: "UDP is worse": no, it's chosen on purpose when speed matters more (games, video, DNS).
port.f.routage.enfant: The lighthouses pass the light along, one to the next, up to the right machine.
port.f.routage.grands: Routing: each router picks the next hop from its table; the TTL limits the number of hops.
port.f.routage.limite: The path can change for each packet, and the way there and back can take different paths.
port.f.routage.idee: "A message goes straight from one computer to the other": no, it hops from router to router.
port.f.box_nat.enfant: The home router is the building caretaker: it gives each device a number and sorts the mail.
port.f.box_nat.grands: The home router acts as gateway, DHCP server (private addresses) and NAT (a single public address for the whole home).
port.f.box_nat.limite: Wi-Fi isn't "the Internet": it's only the last metre between your device and the router.
port.f.box_nat.idee: "My 192.168… address is my address on the Internet": no, the Internet sees the router's public address.
port.f.tls.enfant: The envelope sealed with wax, with a seal checked by the notary.
port.f.tls.grands: HTTPS = HTTP inside TLS: the trip is encrypted and the certificate is signed by an authority, in the site's name.
port.f.tls.limite: The padlock proves WHO you're talking to, not that the site is honest.
port.f.tls.idee: "A site with a padlock is always safe": no, a deceptive site can have a real certificate too.
port.meuble.panneau:
⚓ THE MESSENGER HARBOUR
Welcome, {nom}!
Here, every biome of the Terminaworld is a machine with an address.
The base camp is you: localhost, 127.0.0.1.
The Root is the great router: messengers go through it.
Read the directory (annuaire.txt), keep your logbook (carnet_de_bord.txt)
and light your lantern on your dock (quai/).
— The harbour captain

port.meuble.teleporteur:
THE TELEPORTER (ssh)
To go into another machine you need a key pair:
- the secret key stays with you, always;
- the padlock (the public key) goes on the machine you visit.
On arrival, the machine sets a challenge only your secret key can solve.
No password travels.

hista.port1.1.dit: And your address? The phone's network cards: `ifconfig`. Look for lo and 127.0.0.1.
hista.port1.1.bravo: lo is the loop: a card that only leads back to the phone itself. 127.0.0.1 is your base camp: localhost.
hista.port1.1.adulte: `ifconfig` (the old command, replaced by `ip a` on Linux computers) lists the interfaces; lo is the loopback, 127.0.0.1/8.
hista.port2.1.dit: Ask for the address of the name localhost: `nslookup localhost`.
hista.port2.1.bravo: Answer: 127.0.0.1. The directory found the name's address.
hista.port2.1.adulte: Here `nslookup` is a Terminagotchi command: it resolves localhost and the Terminaworld names, without ever querying the Internet.
hista.port4.0.dit: The ssh teleporter doesn't exist on the phone. Listen to its story: `port teleporteur`.
hista.port4.0.bravo: A secret key that never travels, a padlock you can show everyone.
hista.port4.0.adulte: On a computer, `ssh-keygen` makes the pair; the public key goes into ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on the target machine.
hista.port4.1.dit: The story is also written on the dock: `cat teleporteur.txt`.
hista.port4.1.bravo: Keep it in mind: you'll make your real key pair on a computer.
hista.port4.1.adulte: An asymmetric key pair: what the public key can verify, only the private key can produce.
hista.port5.1.bravo: Your lantern shines at dock 8000, only inside the phone (127.0.0.1).
hista.port5.1.adulte: `serveur` is a small Terminagotchi HTTP server: it serves the quai folder and only listens on 127.0.0.1; no other machine can reach it.
hista.port5.3.bravo: Lantern out. A server you no longer use should be stopped: one less open door.
hista.port5.3.adulte: Stopping a useless service closes a door: fewer open doors, fewer risks.
hista.port7.0.bravo: Each LISTEN line is an open door: an address, a colon, a door number.
hista.port7.0.adulte: Here `ss` is a Terminagotchi command: it shows the doors the app opens (lighthouse 8042, lantern 8000), all on 127.0.0.1. On a computer, `ss -tln` shows them all.
hista.port9.0.bravo: For every Terminaworld machine: which lighthouse to go through, and in how many hops.
hista.port9.0.adulte: On a computer, `ip route` shows the real routing table; here, the one of the simulated Terminaworld network.
hista.port9.1.dit: Read the messengers' lifetime: `ping -c 3 127.0.0.1`, then look at ttl=.
hista.port9.1.bravo: ttl=64: the messenger could still pass 64 lighthouses before vanishing.
hista.port9.1.adulte: The TTL (time to live) drops by 1 at each router; at 0 the packet is dropped. Linux starts at 64.
